newsitem.title: TAIWAN: U.S. official urges wider Taiwan role in economy.
newsitem.headline: U.S. official urges wider Taiwan role in economy.

text.p: U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers used a rare visit to Taiwan on Monday to hail the island's powerhouse economy and to urge it to play a wider international role in Asia.
"I also look forward to the day when we can welcome Taiwan into the World Trade Organisation," Summers told the American Chamber of Commerce in a luncheon speech.

Praising Taiwan's dramatic development in recent decades and its drive to liberalise its financial system, Summers called the island an "economic powerhouse" and -- alluding to its rivalry with China -- said Taiwan had a role to play in the WTO.

"I recognise there are political issues, but I nevertheless see it as a golden opportunity for Taiwan to increase its role in this important international organisation, and to play the part that it should as a major Asian economy," Summers said.
China, which has regarded Taiwan as a rebel province since a civil war split them in 1949, says the island is not entitled to membership as a sovereign nation in international bodies.
Beijing has said it would accept Taiwan's membership in the WTO as a customs territory, but not before China itself is allowed to join the world trade club.
The United States, Canada, Europe and Japan have cited China's market barriers in excluding it from the WTO.
Summers is the highest-ranking U.S. official to visit Taiwan since Transportation Secretary Federico Pena in December 1994.
His delegation met economics vice minister Hsu Ke-sheng and other financial and foreign affairs officials for wide-ranging talks that included bilateral and regional economic issues.

Beijing suggested last week that it would be unhappy about such meetings, reminding Washington that its establishment of diplomatic ties with China included a promise to have no official relations with Taiwan, including high-level visits.
The United States switched diplomatic recognition to Beijing from Taipei in 1979 but keeps close, unofficial trade ties with Taiwan and has sought since 1994 to bolster economic relations.
Taiwanese state radio reported on Monday that Summers had promised Washington's help with Taiwan's expeditious WTO entry at a meeting with economics minister Wang Chih-kang.
Wang pledged to try to solve bilateral trade frictions.
"Vice Minister Summers thinks there are still problems in medical equipment (imports), and the Economics Ministry promises to seek for reasonable solutions," Wang said on the radio.
U.S. medical equipment makers have accused Taiwan of blocking exports to the island by imposing special requirements on local importers.
"If necessary, we will send a team to the United States to further discuss with them," Wang said.
Taiwan also would try to further open up its markets and remove investment obstacles, the radio quoted Wang as saying.
Taiwan applied in 1990 to join the WTO's predecessor, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, but is not expected to gain entry before China is allowed to become a member.
